displayName: openshell gateway VM has been running too long — the idle timer did not take it down (#4571)

conditions.displayName: the gateway VM has been up for more than 2 hours

documentation.content:
The OpenShell gateway VM has been running for over two hours. It is designed to be TERMINATED almost always: `openshell-idle-shutdown.timer` shuts it down after four consecutive idle five-minute checks, so the longest legitimate idle-to-off run is about 32 minutes (10-minute boot grace + 20 minutes of strikes + ~2 minutes to stop).

**This is NOT an uptime check and it does not fire when the VM is off.** `uptime_total` only produces samples while the instance runs, so a stopped machine — the normal state — is silent here. That was the reason an uptime check was rejected for this VM: an alert that fires on the normal state trains people to ignore the channel.

**Two causes, both worth knowing:**

1. **The idle timer is broken.** It is the actual cost control. Check `journalctl -t openshell-idle-shutdown` on the VM: it logs a line every five minutes, including `metrics unreadable — state UNKNOWN, strikes reset`, which is the deliberate fail-towards-staying-up path. A gateway whose metrics endpoint is unreachable never accumulates strikes and never shuts down.
2. **Something is genuinely using it for hours.** At ~$0.067/hour against a $5/month cap this is itself worth seeing, since the cap is a runtime budget of roughly 45 hours once the 20 GB disk's ~$2/month standing charge is taken out.

**What already bounds the cost, so this is not an emergency:** the stop-only resource policy `openshell-gateway-nightly-stop` (05:00 Europe/Sofia) ends any runaway within 24 hours, which is about $1.61. The reason to act on the FIRST occurrence is that it recurs nightly if unfixed — three such nights is $4.82 of compute and takes the $5 cap over with the disk included.

The budget's own 50% threshold will also fire, roughly a day later and saying "cost" rather than "the timer did not run".
